mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Mohsen Rafighdoost
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: Iranian journalist and political figure whom John Kiriakou identifies as a co-founder of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the propaganda voice behind the audio tapes distributed in Iran before the 1979 revolution; interviewed on the PBD Podcast, he conceded that the Shah's regime held only 3,000–3,500 political prisoners rather than the 100,000 opposition figures claimed at the time and that the Shah was, in his own judgment, a better man than Ayatollah Khomeini.

data.Per Kiriakou: The propaganda voice of the Iranian Revolution

dyk: … that [Mohsen Rafighdoost](/wiki/mohsen-rafighdoost), whom [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) identifies as a co-founder of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, told a podcast host in Kiriakou's hearing that the [Shah](/wiki/reza-pahlavi)'s regime held only *"3,000–3,500"* political prisoners, not the *"100,000"* the revolutionary opposition claimed?

… that [Mohsen Rafighdoost](/wiki/mohsen-rafighdoost), the pre-recorded propaganda voice used to turn Iranians against the [Shah](/wiki/reza-pahlavi) before the 1979 revolution, later told a podcast host in [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s hearing that the [Shah](/wiki/reza-pahlavi) *"was a better guy than Khomeini"* and that his push to modernise Iran was better than what the Islamic Republic delivered?
mohsen-rafighdoost.body:
**Mohsen Rafighdoost** is an Iranian journalist and political figure whom [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) identifies as a co-founder, alongside Ayatollah Khomeini, of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps after the 1979 Iranian revolution.<Cite t="10:49" /> Kiriakou describes him as the voice that recorded the intro to the pre-revolution propaganda tapes smuggled into Iran to turn the population against the [Shah](/wiki/reza-pahlavi).<Cite t="11:22" />

On the PBD Podcast, Kiriakou notes, Rafighdoost — brought on as *"the propaganda guy"* — was asked point-blank whether the opposition's claim that SAVAK killed 100,000 people had been a lie. In Kiriakou's account of the exchange he heard on tape, Rafighdoost replied that *"many documents have come out"* since, and that *"it was only 3,000, 3,500"* political prisoners under the [Shah](/wiki/reza-pahlavi), not 100,000.<Cite t="11:54" /><Cite t="12:24" /> Rafighdoost went further and offered his personal verdict that *"Shah was a better guy than Khomeini,"* and that the Shah's belief in modernisation of Iran was *"definitely better than [the] Islamic Republic."*<Cite t="12:24" /><Cite t="12:56" />

Kiriakou treats the admission as evidence that a founding figure of the Islamic Republic's security architecture had, four decades on and speaking against interest, effectively conceded that a foundational revolutionary talking point about the [Shah](/wiki/reza-pahlavi)'s prison population had been an exaggeration by roughly a factor of thirty.<Cite t="11:54" />

kiriakou-pardon-request.title: Kiriakou pardon request
kiriakou-pardon-request.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) discovered his own name listed on the prediction market Kalshi as a wagerable contract on whether [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump) would pardon him, with $152,000 of trading volume and about 19–20 percent implied odds, and was blocked from betting on himself for *"conflict of income"*?

events.description: [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) told Patrick Bet-David his implied odds on the Kalshi pardon contract had reached about 19 percent on $152,000 of trading volume, publicising the [pardon request](/wiki/kiriakou-pardon-request).

kiriakou-pardon-request.body:
The **Kiriakou pardon request** is [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s public effort to obtain a presidential pardon from [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump) for the 2013 felony conviction under the [Intelligence Identities Protection Act](/wiki/intelligence-identities-protection-act) that stripped him of his CIA pension, his federal firearm rights and, until an unsolicited pardon from Terry McAuliffe as governor of Virginia, his Virginia voting rights.<Cite t="1:19:19" /><Cite t="1:20:23" />

## What he wants back

Asked what a federal pardon would actually change, Kiriakou reduced it to two items: *"It would give me my pension back … and give me my gun rights back, Pat. I want my guns back."*<Cite t="1:19:19" /> He said he lost his federal voting rights for life on top of that but has already recovered them at the state level: unprompted, Terry McAuliffe sent a courier to his Virginia house at seven in the morning with a hardcover envelope containing a state pardon decree bearing the gold seal, without Kiriakou ever meeting the man.<Cite t="1:20:23" /><Cite t="1:20:54" /> He notes the state pardon restores his Virginia gun rights but does not shield him from the federal felon-with-a-firearm charge, which carries a five-year mandatory minimum.<Cite t="1:21:27" /> If pardoned, Kiriakou said, he and his children have already planned to *"pile in the car"* and drive to the gun show at the Dulles Airport Expo Center *"with wads of cash"* to buy firearms.<Cite t="1:19:51" />

## The Mar-a-Lago encounter

Kiriakou said he went to Mar-a-Lago with a friend for lunch about a year and a half before the interview and found himself in the same room as Trump, who was dining with Mark Zuckerberg.<Cite t="1:17:48" /> When Trump rose and approached his table, Kiriakou stood up and used what he called his *"go-to line"*: *"Mr President, my name's John Kiriakou. I'm the CIA torture whistleblower. [Barack Obama](/wiki/barack-obama) and [John Brennan](/wiki/john-brennan) ruined my life, and you're the only person who can give it back to me."* Trump replied *"[Tucker Carlson](/wiki/tucker-carlson) told me about you"* and instructed him to *"talk to [Pam Bondi](/wiki/pam-bondi), she'll get the paperwork done."*<Cite t="1:18:18" /><Cite t="1:18:49" /> Kiriakou said he never obtained direct access to Bondi and worked instead through *"a friend of a friend of a friend"* and through the US pardon attorney, Ed Martin.<Cite t="1:18:49" />

## Letters and public advocates

Kiriakou credits [Tucker Carlson](/wiki/tucker-carlson), Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr Phil with writing letters of support for the pardon petition.<Cite t="1:18:49" />

## The Kalshi contract

On 22 April 2026 Kiriakou discovered that the prediction market Kalshi had opened a contract on whether Trump would pardon him.<Cite t="1:15:45" /> He said his implied odds were about 20 percent one day, 19 percent the next, on $152,000 of trading volume, and that when he tried to place a twenty-dollar bet on himself the platform blocked the trade for *"conflict of income."*<Cite t="1:16:45" /><Cite t="1:17:16" />

splc-2025-indictment.title: SPLC 2025 indictment
splc-2025-indictment.summary: Federal criminal case unveiled by FBI director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche against the Southern Poverty Law Center on multiple felony counts, described by John Kiriakou as concerning alleged payments to the Ku Klux Klan and Nazi groups and alleged money laundering; Kiriakou judges the charges are of the documentary kind that either happened or did not and that they could bring an end to an organisation whose 2024 balance sheet showed assets of roughly $786 to $822 million.

data.Alleged conduct: Payments to the Ku Klux Klan and Nazi groups; money laundering

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said the felony indictment of the Southern Poverty Law Center announced by [FBI](/wiki/fbi) director Kash Patel alleges the group *"gave money to the Ku Klux Klan"* and *"gave money to Nazi groups"* and involves *"very clear laws"* on money laundering — and that if the paperwork is real *"this could be the end of the [SPLC](/wiki/splc-2025-indictment)"*?

… that in 2024 the Southern Poverty Law Center's total assets stood at roughly $786.7 million — some reports put the figure at $822 million — with $106 million in donations that year alone, funded in part, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) notes on the [SPLC indictment](/wiki/splc-2025-indictment), by Tim Cook, George Soros and the Charles Schwab and Fidelity charitable foundations?
splc-2025-indictment.body:
The **SPLC 2025 indictment** is the federal criminal case that [FBI](/wiki/fbi) director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche unveiled against the Southern Poverty Law Center on multiple felony counts. [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said his first reaction on seeing the push notification was dismissive — *"Oh, come on, we have nothing better to do"* — but that reading the underlying article changed his mind: *"These are real crimes. The kind of crimes where they're documentary. You either did it or you didn't do it. And if they've got documentary evidence that they did it, this could be the end of the SPLC."*<Cite t="1:23:34" /><Cite t="1:24:35" />

## The alleged conduct

Kiriakou characterises the underlying allegations as *"giving money to the Ku Klux Klan, giving money to Nazi groups, you know, laundering money."* He calls the money-laundering statutes *"very clear"* and *"very specific"* and dismisses the SPLC's public rebuttal — that any payments were the equivalent of a journalist buying a share of stock to attend a shareholder meeting — as *"weak."*<Cite t="1:25:06" /><Cite t="1:25:37" />

## Scale

Kiriakou recites the SPLC's 2024 balance sheet — total assets of $786.7 million, with some reports putting the figure at $822 million, and $106 million in donations that year — and names among the donors Tim Cook at a million dollars, George Soros, George Clooney, the Charles Schwab Charitable Foundation and Fidelity Charitable.<Cite t="1:28:43" /><Cite t="1:30:18" /> He draws a wider lesson about the drift of endowments away from their founders' original causes and says the case underscores why he read Form 990 disclosures obsessively as chief investigator for the [Senate Foreign Relations Committee](/wiki/senate-foreign-relations-committee): *"the 990s will tell you everything you need to know about an organisation that you're targeting."*<Cite t="1:28:43" />

## Hate map coverage

Kiriakou notes that the SPLC's hate map has included Moms for Liberty, Moms for America and Turning Point USA among its listed groups while excluding Antifa, and credits the libertarian commentator John Stossel with early reporting on SPLC's use of offshore accounts in the Cayman Islands drawn from its Form 990.<Cite t="1:26:38" /><Cite t="1:27:09" /><Cite t="1:27:40" />

christopher-hitchens.title: Christopher Hitchens
christopher-hitchens.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, famously argued in the mid-2000s that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' agreed in 2008 to undergo a filmed waterboarding demonstration, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and thereafter suffered panic attacks for the rest of his life whenever he could not breathe for a moment.

data.Per Kiriakou: The most cited celebrity self-experiment on waterboarding

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says [Christopher Hitchens](/wiki/christopher-hitchens), who had once dismissed [waterboarding](/wiki/waterboarding) as nothing, tapped out of his 2008 filmed demonstration after about *seventeen seconds* and thereafter suffered panic attacks for the rest of his life whenever he could not breathe for a moment?

… that [Christopher Hitchens](/wiki/christopher-hitchens) is the celebrity data point [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) reaches for when non-specialists insist [waterboarding](/wiki/waterboarding) is *"not torture"* — *"Believe me, it's torture"*?
christopher-hitchens.body:
**Christopher Hitchens** was a British-American journalist and author whose 2008 filmed self-experiment with [waterboarding](/wiki/waterboarding) [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) treats as the canonical rebuttal to those who describe the technique as *"not a big deal."*<Cite t="1:22:29" /><Cite t="1:23:34" /> Kiriakou recounts the sequence: Hitchens was placed on his back, a towel was laid across his face, and he expressed misplaced confidence he would be able to breathe. He lasted, in Kiriakou's telling, about *"seventeen seconds"* before he jumped up.<Cite t="1:22:29" />

What mattered more to Kiriakou than the length of the demonstration was what followed. *"For the rest of his life, every time he couldn't breathe for a second, he would have panic attacks. Because of the impact of waterboarding had on him."*<Cite t="1:23:01" /> Kiriakou closes the anecdote with the point he says the corollary makes on the non-specialists: *"Believe me, it's torture."*<Cite t="1:23:34" />

cia-political-neutrality-tradition.title: CIA political neutrality tradition
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.summary: The informal midcentury norm at the Central Intelligence Agency, described by John Kiriakou from his own 1990-era experience, under which employees did not share their partisan affiliations at work, small displays such as a Bob Dole campaign bumper sticker in a cubicle triggered severe internal discipline, and career officers steered clear of political endorsement — a tradition Kiriakou argues collapsed by 2020, when 51 former intelligence officials signed the letter dismissing the Hunter Biden laptop story.

data.Per Kiriakou: Broken by the 2020 Hunter Biden laptop letter

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) recalls a colleague at the [CIA](/wiki/cia) who put up a small Bob Dole bumper sticker in her cubicle in 1996 being suspended a week without pay, denied promotion for a year, and given a formal reprimand — and *"walking out balling"* — for violating the [agency's political-neutrality norm](/wiki/cia-political-neutrality-tradition)?

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says he had *"literally no idea"* of the partisan affiliations of the colleagues he sat with ten hours a day at the [CIA](/wiki/cia) in the 1990s — a [norm](/wiki/cia-political-neutrality-tradition) he says was blown apart when 51 former intelligence officials signed the 2020 letter calling the Hunter Biden laptop *"Russian disinformation"*?
cia-political-neutrality-tradition.body:
The **CIA political neutrality tradition** is the informal norm, described by [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) from his 1990s [CIA](/wiki/cia) career, under which employees kept their partisan affiliations invisible at work and any breach was treated as a serious violation.<Cite t="1:12:38" /> Kiriakou says he sat with people ten hours a day *"and had literally no idea"* of their political affiliations: *"It never came up. It never needed to come up. We were there to serve the American people."*<Cite t="1:12:38" />

## The Bob Dole sticker incident

In 1996, Kiriakou recalls, a colleague sat about three cubicles down from him and *"very discreetly"* put up a small Bob Dole for President bumper sticker in her cubicle. Management, he says, *"came down on her like a ton of bricks."* She was suspended for a week without pay, denied promotion for a year, and issued a formal letter in her file finding that she had violated agency regulations. Kiriakou remembers her *"balling as she was walking out."*<Cite t="1:13:10" /><Cite t="1:13:41" />

## Collapse of the norm

By 2020, Kiriakou argues, the norm was gone. He notes that of the 51 former intelligence officials who signed the public letter dismissing the Hunter Biden laptop as *"Russian disinformation,"* he personally knew *"every single one"* and considers that *"every single one of them was working for [Hillary Clinton](/wiki/hillary-clinton), either directly or indirectly."* On his account, [John Brennan](/wiki/john-brennan) himself emerged as *"a nobody around 2007"* only because a mass retirement of senior CIA officers after 9/11 sorted broadly fifty-fifty between the Hillary Clinton and John McCain campaigns, and Brennan was, by his account, *"the only one that went to the [Obama](/wiki/barack-obama) campaign."*<Cite t="1:14:11" /><Cite t="1:14:42" /><Cite t="1:15:13" />

Kiriakou argues the political drift of the retired-officer class is why the 51 signatories should never have retained security clearances after leaving the agency, and why [Donald Trump](/wiki/donald-trump)'s first-term suspension of those clearances was justified.<Cite t="1:12:05" /><Cite t="1:12:38" />
